name: Haemolytic disease of the newborn
aliases: haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

clinicalPearls: Immune haemolysis of fetal and neonatal red cells caused by maternal alloantibodies crossing the placenta
Rhesus D incompatibility historically caused severe disease; ABO incompatibility is now a common but usually milder cause
Other antibodies such as anti-Kell can cause severe disease, partly by suppressing erythropoiesis
Antenatally it can cause fetal anaemia and hydrops; postnatally it causes early, rapidly rising jaundice and anaemia
The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the baby is typically positive in immune haemolysis
Routine anti-D prophylaxis has greatly reduced rhesus disease; management includes phototherapy, exchange transfusion and, antenatally, intrauterine transfusion
reference.pathophysiology: Haemolytic disease of the newborn occurs when maternal IgG alloantibodies, formed against fetal red cell antigens the mother lacks, cross the placenta and bind fetal red cells, leading to their destruction by the reticuloendothelial system. The resulting fetal anaemia can cause high-output failure and hydrops in severe cases. After birth, continued haemolysis produces anaemia and a rapid rise in unconjugated bilirubin, which, if untreated, can cross the immature blood-brain barrier and cause kernicterus. Anti-Kell disease additionally suppresses fetal erythropoiesis.
additionalDifferentials: Non-immune haemolysis (for example G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis)
Internal haemorrhage (for example cephalohaematoma, intracranial bleed)
additionalInvestigations: Maternal antibody screening and identification antenatally
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the neonate
Blood group and film of the newborn
Antenatal monitoring of fetal anaemia (for example middle cerebral artery Doppler)
redFlags: Hydrops fetalis or severe fetal anaemia
Rapidly rising bilirubin approaching exchange-transfusion thresholds
reference.prognosis: With prophylaxis, antenatal monitoring and modern neonatal treatment, outcomes are usually good, but severe untreated disease can cause hydrops, kernicterus or death, and late anaemia may require follow-up.
pitfalls: Missing rapidly rising jaundice in the first day of life
Overlooking late anaemia after apparent recovery
Failing to give appropriate anti-D prophylaxis to at-risk mothers
